source_read: PMC HTML (PMC6191498; Front Psychiatry 2018;9:491): abstract, all background sections (methamphetamine, acute and chronic methamphetamine psychosis, schizophrenia, relationship), review aims/inclusion/search, positive, negative and cognitive symptom sections, Table 1 and Table 2 (read as tables), limitations, summary and conclusions with Figure 1 legend, author contributions, conflict of interest, acknowledgments, and reference-list entries for every source behind the claim figures (refs 34-37, 49-56, 91-94, 105-140).

claims.overstatement: None from this source; but the claim's 'otherwise treatment rests on case reports and on evidence from other psychoses' is contradicted in part: this review cites a randomized controlled trial of aripiprazole versus risperidone in amphetamine-induced psychosis (Farnia et al., 2014, Am J Drug Alcohol Abuse 40:s10-15; ref 140) that the claim does not mention. Whether its participants used methamphetamine is not stated in this review.
claims.note: This source supports only the general point that randomized evidence is limited: its treatment paragraph is explicitly 'not clinical recommendations' and calls for large randomized trials. The 2009 Cochrane review, its single 58-participant olanzapine-haloperidol trial and the haloperidol-quetiapine trial are not mentioned here. Also cited: one case report of electroconvulsive therapy for persistent psychosis (Grelotti 2010, ref 54).

anchors.extracted: Authors suggest acute psychosis resolves with abstinence and withdrawal management so long-term drug treatment is mostly not needed (citing a StatPearls chapter); for persistent psychosis, given similarity to schizophrenia, second-generation antipsychotics 'may be appropriate'; first-generation agents such as haloperidol carry elevated extrapyramidal risk in methamphetamine-induced psychosis (citing Cadet and Gold 2018 and the Farnia 2014 RCT of aripiprazole vs risperidone in amphetamine-induced psychosis). States these are not clinical recommendations and need large randomized trials.

claims.overstatement: None in direction. Several specific figures in the claim are not in this source: '16-17% still psychotic after 1-3 months in two small studies' (this review instead gives 15-28% of hospitalized patients still needing hospitalization beyond 2-3 months, and 'up to 30%' with symptoms up to 6 months), the Thai cohort's size (>1,000) and the '5-6 years' window (this review: 38.8% at 5-year follow-up), and 'recurrence with renewed use is common' (not stated here).
claims.note: Supported from this source: most episodes resolve within about a month of stopping; a minority persist (10-28% beyond 6 months in Japanese hospital series); later schizophrenia diagnoses 5.0% (China) to 38.8% at 5 years (Thailand), and 19.1-30% after amphetamine-induced psychosis in register studies. The authors caution that such transitions may partly reflect diagnostic convention (they state, apparently inaccurately, that DSM-5 requires a primary-psychosis diagnosis after 6 months; DSM-5's substance-induced criterion refers to persistence of about 1 month after cessation - editors' note). All figures are second-hand.

anchors.extracted: Typically transient; most symptoms resolve within 1 month (Sato 1992; Deng 2012). Up to 30% with symptoms up to 6 months after abstinence (Deng 2012); 15-28% of those admitted with methamphetamine psychosis needing hospitalization for more than 2-3 months (Iwanami 1994; Nakatani 1989); 10-28% psychotic for more than 6 months (Ujike and Sato 2004; Iwanami 1994); 28% with 'schizophrenia-like symptoms' 8-12 years after abstinence (Teraoka 1967); 7% risk of psychotic symptoms in abstinent users (McKetin 2013); 5% of abstinent dependent users with a psychotic disorder at 3 years (Glasner-Edwards 2010).

anchors.locator: The relationship between METH-induced psychosis and schizophrenia, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Thai patients first hospitalized for methamphetamine psychosis: 38.8% diagnosed with schizophrenia at 5-year follow-up (Kittirattanapaiboon 2010). 5.0% of Chinese patients had diagnosis changed to schizophrenia (Deng 2012). 19.1% (Alderson) to 30% (Niemi-Pynttari 2013) transition to schizophrenia after amphetamine-induced psychosis; California cohort: higher risk of later schizophrenia after methamphetamine-related hospitalization (Callaghan 2012).

anchors.locator: The relationship between METH-induced psychosis and schizophrenia, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Authors: because diagnostic rules require a primary-psychosis diagnosis when psychosis persists (stated as beyond 6 months), schizophrenia diagnoses after methamphetamine psychosis may reflect diagnostic protocol rather than the true course.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim is more cautious than the review's abstract, which says acute methamphetamine psychosis 'could be clinically distinguished' from primary psychosis by behavioural and cognitive features; the claim's 'symptoms alone do not reliably separate the two' matches the body and limitations. 'Samples of 22-285' reproduces Table 1's n column, which overstates the compared groups for some studies (Medhus 2013: n 285 printed, comparison 9 vs 33; Srisurapanont 2011: n 61 printed, groups 168 vs 169).
claims.note: Table 1 lists 12 directly comparative studies, Tomiyama 1990 to McKetin 2017; Table 2 adds a 13th (Hajebi 2018). Chen et al. 2015: BPRS total and positive scores equal in persistent methamphetamine psychosis and schizophrenia, both above acute (Table 1); the review's text describes the same comparison as PANSS. Visual/tactile hallucination differences rest mainly on one direct comparison (Wang 2016) and indirect comparisons.

anchors.extracted: 12 studies directly comparing methamphetamine psychosis with schizophrenia/primary psychosis, published 1990 (Tomiyama) to 2017 (McKetin); printed n 22 to 285. Printed n disagrees with the listed groups for Medhus 2013 (285 vs 33 + 9), Srisurapanont 2011 (61 vs 168 + 169) and Chen 2015 ('160 METH users' vs 25 + 50 + 56 = 131).

anchors.locator: Positive symptoms > Acute meth psychosis vs. schizophrenia, paras 2-4
anchors.extracted: No difference in type/severity of positive symptoms on PANSS or BPRS in several acute comparisons; Hajebi 2018: similar positive symptoms at admission, discharge, 6 and 12 months; Srisurapanont 2011: incoherent speech the only differentiating item; Shelly 2016: voices conversing 48.5% vs 20.3%, thought broadcasting 24% vs 42% (significant only after age adjustment). Authors: initial presentation indistinguishable.

anchors.locator: Positive symptoms > final para of acute section; Chronic meth psychosis vs. schizophrenia, para 1; Table 1 (Wang 2016)
anchors.extracted: Wang 2016 (53 vs 53, psychosis >1 month after stopping): same delusion patterns, auditory hallucinations commonest in both, visual and tactile hallucinations more prevalent in methamphetamine psychosis, conceptual disorganization more in schizophrenia. Indirect data: visual hallucinations 46.5% and tactile 21.3% in one methamphetamine psychosis sample vs 16-27% visual in schizophrenia. Authors note these rest largely on indirect comparisons.

Milder negative symptoms in methamphetamine psychosis: Tomiyama 1990 (11 vs 11; affective flattening and alogia), Wang 2016 (blunted affect, emotional withdrawal, motor retardation), Chen 2015 (BPRS negative schizophrenia > persistent > acute), Hajebi 2018 (at admission and discharge). No difference in Srisurapanont 2011, Hides 2015 (BPRS) and Okada 2016 (PANSS).

anchors.locator: Table 1 (Chen 2015; McKetin 2017); Cognitive symptoms > Chronic, para 2
anchors.extracted: Chen 2015 (5 groups, Taiwan): persistent psychosis (>1 month after abstinence) equal to schizophrenia on BPRS total and positive scores and on all BACS cognitive measures, both worse than acute psychosis, users without psychosis and controls. McKetin 2017 (284): no difference between persistent methamphetamine psychosis and primary psychosis on any lifetime positive symptom.

anchors.locator: Methodological limitations, paras 1-3; Summary and conclusions, paras 1 and 3; Abstract
anchors.extracted: Most studies did not report abstinence, did not separate acute from chronic psychosis, had small samples, did not control polydrug use or medication, and used brief scales that may miss qualitative differences. Summary: difficult to distinguish clinically on positive symptoms alone; insufficient evidence to say whether chronic methamphetamine psychosis is distinct. Abstract nonetheless suggests acute methamphetamine psychosis could be clinically distinguished.

key_findings.correction: Odds ratios recomputed: voices conversing 3.70 (1.5-9.1); thought broadcasting 2.27 (0.9-5.7).

reporting_issues.note: Table 1 row 109 vs Positive symptoms > Chronic, 3rd paragraph vs Figure 1 legend footnote b.

Relationship section (paras 1 and 3) says >6 months; Methodological limitations para 2 implies >1 month. Editors' note: DSM-5's substance-induced criterion refers to persistence for about 1 month after cessation.
Yamamuro inconsistency found independently; Okada (15 of 21 residual/late-onset per Table 2) and Srisurapanont (Table 2 'could represent both') confirmed.
Both terms appear in the same cognitive paragraph; abstract and summary say selective.
Ref 41: McKetin, Kelly, McLaren 2006, crystalline methamphetamine use and dependence; ref 135: Bobes et al., cardiovascular risk and smoking in the CLAMORS schizophrenia cohort.
A reading limitation rather than a reporting issue of the paper; belongs in source_read.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low (no protocol, no excluded-study list, single reviewer).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: abstract's claim that acute methamphetamine psychosis could be clinically distinguished outruns the body, which calls the key evidence indirect.

missed: The management paragraph (Summary and conclusions, 3rd paragraph) cites a randomized controlled trial of aripiprazole versus risperidone in amphetamine-induced psychosis (Farnia et al., 2014, Am J Drug Alcohol Abuse 40:s10-15; ref 140). Not on the card; relevant to cl_meth_psychosis_treatment, which says that apart from the Cochrane trial and one later haloperidol-quetiapine trial, treatment rests on case reports and evidence from other psychoses.

For cl_meth_psychosis_course: this review does not contain the claim's '16-17% still psychotic after 1-3 months', the Thai cohort size, or 'recurrence with renewed use'; its own 2-3-month figure is 15-28% still hospitalized, and it gives 'up to 30%' with symptoms to 6 months (Deng 2012).
